title: TypeScript SDK: streaming-friendly typegen with cross-chunk discriminated unions and dual Zod/AJV output
creator: Maya Chen
description:
Problem: the current TypeScript SDK typegen emits complete discriminated unions and JSON-schema/Zod artifacts assuming the model response is produced as a single chunk. For streaming responses (token-by-token or chunked JSON) consumers must stitch partial payloads and then validate — this creates brittle client-side code and incorrect runtime validation coverage.

This ticket introduces a streaming-first type generation pipeline that: 1) emits a compact shape registry that supports incremental reconstruction of discriminated unions across chunk boundaries, 2) produces both Zod validators and AJV-compatible JSON Schemas from the same canonical shape definitions, and 3) exposes lean runtime adapters on the SDK to rehydrate and validate streaming outputs with minimal overhead.
background: Past work produced full-schema generators and several streaming helpers, but we still see two recurring issues in customer reports: (a) validators reject streaming outputs that are validated chunk-by-chunk because the discriminator only appears at the end or across chunks, and (b) teams need both runtime Zod validators (for local dev) and AJV schemas (for server-side strict validation) but the generation step duplicates logic and drifts. See customer incident INC-2201 and design notes in Confluence: https://company.atlassian.net/l/cp/tsdk-streaming-shapes
goals:
- Allow SDK users to validate streamed structured outputs robustly without buffering whole responses in memory.
- Provide a single source-of-truth shape registry that emits: TypeScript types, Zod validators, and AJV JSON Schemas.
- Add a minimal runtime adapter (StreamReconstructor) that stitches chunks, infers discriminators, and performs incremental validation with configurable strictness.
scope:
In scope: typegen transforms, Zod + AJV emitters, StreamReconstructor API, examples and a migration guide.
Out of scope: rewriting all existing tSDK clients to use the new adapter (we will provide opt-in examples and adapters for common patterns).
acceptance_criteria: Typegen emits a shape registry JSON file for a model output with discriminated unions (example included) and corresponding .d.ts with union types.
Zod and AJV artifacts are generated from the same canonical shapes and pass the same unit tests for the sample corpus.
StreamReconstructor can assemble a union type where the discriminator token appears in any chunk boundary (unit + integration tests).
End-to-end example shows streaming chat response validated incrementally with <= 3KB extra memory compared to fully-buffered validation for typical 2k token messages.
Documentation with migration notes and an example repo (tsdk-examples/streaming-validate) exists and links are in PR description.
technical_design:
Key pieces: (1) Canonical Shape Registry: small JSON representation with nodes (object, array, primitive, discriminator-hint) and stable IDs. (2) Generator: consumes registry -> emits TypeScript types + Zod factories + AJV JSON Schema per node. Zod emit uses lazy() + refinements to support incremental partial validation. AJV emit includes 'unevaluatedProperties' hints to enable streaming checks. (3) StreamReconstructor: event-driven builder with three modes: permissive (logs mismatches), strict (throws at first mismatch), and recover (attempts to map partial fields to union variant using heuristic ranking). (4) Discriminator heuristics: prefer explicit tagged field ("type", "kind"); fall back to shape-score (presence of unique keys). Heuristics are recorded in emitted metadata so consumers can opt-in to deterministic resolution.

Performance tradeoffs: full validation on every chunk is expensive. We adopt an incremental algorithm: validate only fields present in chunk and maintain a per-candidate validation state; run full union disambiguation only when a discriminator appears or when message end is signaled. This balances CPU and memory.

Edge-cases: streaming with out-of-order chunks or missing delimiters — StreamReconstructor will expose callbacks so higher-level protocols (SSE/WebSocket) can supply boundary markers.

Compatibility: generator keeps backward compatibility with previous single-file schema output; output artifact names use new suffix "-stream" to allow coexistence.
implementation_notes: Step 1: Extend typegen IR with 'discriminator_hints' and 'stream_fragment' flags (generator changes only).
Step 2: Add Zod emitter support for 'lazy' validators and incremental partial-validate api: z.object(...).partial().safeParseSyncPartial(dataChunk).
Step 3: Add AJV emitter that outputs JSON Schema with 'x-stream-hints' vendor extension for runtime reconstructor to use, and support compile time roundtrip tests.
Step 4: Implement StreamReconstructor in src/stream-reconstructor.ts with modes: permissive|strict|recover and an event API: on('variantResolved', cb), on('partialValidation', cb).
Step 5: Write integration tests that run a local streaming mock model server which sends chunked JSON split at arbitrary byte boundaries. Use sample prompts to cover variant inference.
migration_notes: Migration is opt-in: existing consumers keep current behavior. To migrate: 1) regenerate shapes with 'tsdk typegen --stream' 2) import StreamReconstructor and replace buffered validator usage with incremental flow: const recon = new StreamReconstructor({mode: 'recover', schemaPath: './shapes-stream.json'}); recon.feedChunk(chunk); recon.on('variantResolved', (v) => { // application logic });

prs: GH-1234: feature(typegen): emit shape registry + zod/ajv artifacts
review_feedback: Design review (2025-01-20) — Josh B. recommended recording deterministic tie-breakers for heuristic decisions (added metadata field 'heuristic_resolution_order').
Security review flagged AJV 'unevaluatedProperties' usage; we'll gate strict schema emit behind a flag until we get a perf/security audit (see 'security_action' comment).
DX review: request for a tiny starter example (<=25 lines) for README — assigned to Luis.
open_questions: Should StreamReconstructor be exported from the top-level package or from a new workspace '@redwood/tsdk-stream' to avoid tree-shaking regressions?
Do we include synchronous partial-validate APIs or only async (Promise) variants for Zod/AJV? Current plan: provide both, prefer sync for small chunks.
What default mode should server-side SDKs use: strict or recover? Recommend 'recover' for hosted->customer code paths to avoid 5xx when model output drifts.
notes: Performance target: reconstructor must add <5ms CPU per 1k tokens on p3.xlarge emulator for permissive mode (bench TBD).
Customer ask: ACME search team wants streaming validation to avoid re-parsing 2MB JSON payloads — include a sample using Node streams.
